notes.meaning: Jesus was in Jerusalem during the Feast of Dedication, a festival held in winter. Today called Hanukkah, this celebration remembered how the temple was cleansed and dedicated again to God after an enemy ruler had ruined it. The cold winter weather set the scene for the tense conversation that followed.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church fathers like Augustine noted that the mention of winter also painted a picture of the leaders' cold hearts, which refused the warmth of God's love.

notes.meaning: Jesus walked along Solomon's Colonnade, a covered porch on the east side of the temple courts. Its high roof and sturdy walls gave shelter from the winter wind and rain. It was a well-known gathering spot where people could walk and talk comfortably together.

A crowd of Jewish leaders surrounded Jesus and demanded that he speak without riddles. They asked how long he would keep them in suspense and told him to say plainly if he was the Messiah, the promised rescuer sent by God. They did not ask to learn, but hoped to trap him into saying something they could use to arrest him.

Jesus replied that he had already told them who he was, but they refused to trust him. He pointed to his miracles, which he carried out in his Father's name and by his Father's authority. Those mighty works were clear evidence proving his divine mission.

Jesus told the leaders that their lack of faith was not caused by missing proof, but by the fact that they were not his sheep. Their stubborn pride and love of praise kept them from having the teachable heart of a true disciple. Because they refused his guidance, they remained outside his flock.

Jesus described what marks his genuine followers. His sheep listen to his voice with faith, he knows and loves each of them personally, and they obediently follow where he leads. True faith shows itself in hearing and trusting the Good Shepherd.

Jesus promises to give his sheep eternal life, which is a life with God that begins now and lasts forever. He guarantees that they will never be destroyed in hell. No thief, enemy, or power can rip them out of his protective hand.

differ.view: Southern Baptists understand this promise to mean that a true believer can never lose their salvation. In their official statement of faith, they teach that everyone truly accepted by Christ and renewed by the Holy Spirit will stay faithful to the end and never fall away from God's grace (His free gift of salvation).

The Assemblies of God teaches that while no outside enemy can steal a Christian from Jesus, a person's security remains tied to ongoing faith. In their official position paper, they state that a believer is fully safe in Christ, but a person can still abandon that salvation by a deliberate choice to walk away.

notes.meaning: The Father is the one who entrusted the sheep to Jesus, and the Father is more powerful than any enemy or created being. Because believers are held by the Father as well, no one can snatch them away. Their ultimate safety rests upon the supreme might of God Himself.

Jesus declared that he and the Father are one. While they are distinct persons within the Godhead, they are united in divine nature, purpose, and power. That equal power guarantees that the flock will never be lost.

When the Jewish leaders heard Jesus speak of being one with the Father, they picked up stones to execute him immediately. Under their law, claiming equality with God was considered blasphemy, a grave sin against God's honor that called for stoning. Their sudden fury proved that they understood exactly what he had claimed.

Jesus stopped the angry crowd by asking a calm question. He pointed out the many kind deeds and miraculous healings he had performed openly by the Father's authority. He asked them to name which of those acts of mercy deserved death by stoning.

The leaders answered that they were not punishing him for doing good works, but for blasphemy. In their eyes, he was merely an ordinary man who was unlawfully claiming to be God. They believed they were defending God's honor by seeking his death.

Jesus directed them back to their own Scriptures by citing Psalm 82, where God said, 'You are gods.' That passage used the title 'gods' for human judges and rulers who were appointed to represent God's justice on earth. Jesus showed that the word was sometimes used in Scripture for those who carry out divine duties.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers claim this verse teaches that believers are small divine beings who have power to speak worlds into existence.

notes.meaning: Jesus argued that the words of Scripture stand firm and can never be broken or set aside. If God could call mortal judges 'gods' simply because his word came to them, the leaders had no right to accuse Jesus of blasphemy. The Father had uniquely consecrated him and sent him into the world, giving him full right to call himself the Son of God.

Jesus told the crowd that if he was not doing the very works of his Father, they had no obligation to believe him. He did not ask them to trust his words blindly without proof. His identity had to be supported by deeds that only God could accomplish.

Even if the leaders struggled to trust his spoken words, Jesus urged them to consider the evidence of his miracles. Looking honestly at those works would help them understand that the Father lives in him and that he lives in the Father. His divine actions pointed directly to his perfect unity with God.

The religious leaders dropped their stones and attempted to seize Jesus to place him on trial, but he slipped away from their grasp. He escaped unharmed through God's power because the appointed time for his suffering had not yet come. No human hostility could cut short his mission before the proper hour.

Jesus left Jerusalem and traveled east across the Jordan River to the area where John the Baptist had first baptized. He stayed there in a quiet region far from the hostile plotting of the religious leaders. This retreat gave him a peaceful place to minister to those who sought him.

Crowds of people came to see Jesus in this countryside location and recalled what John the Baptist had taught. They observed that while John had never worked a miraculous sign, everything John had said about Jesus turned out to be completely true. John's truthful testimony helped open their minds to receive Christ.

Many people in that place believed in Jesus. While the educated leaders in the holy city of Jerusalem had rejected him, ordinary people in the desert region placed their trust in him. John the Baptist's earlier preaching bore rich fruit as many came to living faith.
